stem: A 29-year-old man presents with a 5-year history of recurrent, non-itchy skin lesions. On examination, there are symmetrically distributed, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with thick silvery scales involving the extensor surfaces of the elbows and knees. Oral and genital mucosa are normal, and there is no history of recent infection or drug intake. Based on the clinical pattern and lesion morphology, what is the most likely diagnosis?

keywords: Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with thick silvery scales→ Classic morphological hallmark of chronic plaque psoriasis.
Extensor surfaces (elbows and knees), symmetrical distribution→ Typical site and pattern strongly favors psoriasis over other dermatoses.
Chronic, recurrent course with no mucosal involvement→ Supports psoriasis and helps exclude lichen planus.
keywordsHtml:
1. Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with thick silvery scales
    Classic morphological hallmark of chronic plaque psoriasis.
  2. Extensor surfaces (elbows and knees), symmetrical distribution
    Typical site and pattern strongly favors psoriasis over other dermatoses.
  3. Chronic, recurrent course with no mucosal involvement
    Supports psoriasis and helps exclude lichen planus.

A.title: Chronic plaque psoriasis
A.body:
Chronic plaque psoriasis (Psoriasis Vulgaris) is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by well-demarcated, erythematous (red) plaques covered with characteristic silvery-white scales.
Classic Distribution: It typically affects the extensor surfaces, such as the elbows and knees, the scalp, and the lumbosacral region.
Auspitz Sign: If these scales are scraped off, pinpoint bleeding points often appear, which is a classic clinical sign.
Symmetry: The lesions are usually symmetrically distributed on the body.
Chronic Nature: This patient has a 5-year history, which aligns with the relapsing-remitting nature of the disease. Unlike other inflammatory conditions, it is often asymptomatic or only mildly itchy, rather than intensely pruritic.
Mucosal involvement is uncommon, which supports this diagnosis.
A.bodyHtml:
Chronic plaque psoriasis (Psoriasis Vulgaris) is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by well-demarcated, erythematous (red) plaques covered with characteristic silvery-white scales.

  • Classic Distribution: It typically affects the extensor surfaces, such as the elbows and knees, the scalp, and the lumbosacral region.
  • Auspitz Sign: If these scales are scraped off, pinpoint bleeding points often appear, which is a classic clinical sign.
  • Symmetry: The lesions are usually symmetrically distributed on the body.
  • Chronic Nature: This patient has a 5-year history, which aligns with the relapsing-remitting nature of the disease. Unlike other inflammatory conditions, it is often asymptomatic or only mildly itchy, rather than intensely pruritic.
  • Mucosal involvement is uncommon, which supports this diagnosis.

B.title: Lichen planus
B.body:
Typically presents with violaceous, flat-topped, pruritic papules.
Frequently involves oral and genital mucosa (Wickham striae).
Lesions are more common on flexor surfaces, not extensor areas.❌ Morphology and distribution do not match.
B.bodyHtml:
• Typically presents with violaceous, flat-topped, pruritic papules.
  • Frequently involves oral and genital mucosa (Wickham striae).
  • Lesions are more common on flexor surfaces, not extensor areas.
    ❌ Morphology and distribution do not match.

C.title: Tinea corporis
C.body:
Fungal infection presenting as annular lesions with central clearing and an active scaly border.
Usually itchy and asymmetrical.
Chronic symmetric plaques with silvery scale are not typical.❌ Fungal pattern absent.
C.bodyHtml:
• Fungal infection presenting as annular lesions with central clearing and an active scaly border.
  • Usually itchy and asymmetrical.
  • Chronic symmetric plaques with silvery scale are not typical.
    ❌ Fungal pattern absent.

D.title: Seborrheic dermatitis
D.body:
Involves seborrheic areas (scalp, face, chest).
Lesions have greasy yellow scales, not thick silvery scales.
Extensor surfaces like elbows and knees are usually spared.❌ Distribution and scale type inconsistent.
D.bodyHtml:
• Involves seborrheic areas (scalp, face, chest).
  • Lesions have greasy yellow scales, not thick silvery scales.
  • Extensor surfaces like elbows and knees are usually spared.
    ❌ Distribution and scale type inconsistent.

E.title: Pityriasis rosea
E.body:
Acute, self-limiting condition starting with a herald patch, followed by a Christmas-tree pattern rash.
Commonly affects the trunk, not extensor surfaces.
Usually resolves within 6–8 weeks, not chronic for years.❌ Time course and morphology mismatch.
E.bodyHtml:
• Acute, self-limiting condition starting with a herald patch, followed by a Christmas-tree pattern rash.
  • Commonly affects the trunk, not extensor surfaces.
  • Usually resolves within 6–8 weeks, not chronic for years.
    ❌ Time course and morphology mismatch.

keyConcept: Chronic plaque psoriasis presents with long-standing, symmetrical, well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery scales on extensor surfaces, and minimal mucosal involvement. Recognition of distribution, scale type, and chronicity is crucial for diagnosis.

diagram.name: Chronic Plaque Psoriasis
diagram.caption: This diagram illustrates the classical clinical features of chronic plaque psoriasis, highlighting well-demarcated erythematous plaques with thick silvery scales on extensor surfaces. It also depicts common associations such as nail changes, psoriatic arthritis, the Koebner phenomenon, major triggers, and an overview of treatment options.
